extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, filmmakers, and people preparing treatments for pitching or adapting work
extracted.subtask_description: Creating a prose document that bridges scene cards and a screenplay draft, used either as an internal, detailed draft or as a shorter presentation document for pitching/sales or submissions. Covers tone (present-tense, story-like), scope (draft vs presentation), length, formatting, and use in adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment prose style and tense
rubrics_metrics.description: A film treatment is a piece of prose that reads like a short story, but is told in the present tense and describes events as they happen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the treatment as narrative prose (not screenplay format); use present tense and show events unfolding directly so it conveys story momentum and immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of detail vs outline
rubrics_metrics.description: A treatment is generally longer and more detailed than an outline (or one-page synopsis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include detail beyond a simple synopsis — enough to convey scene beats and character arcs, but vary level depending on whether it is a draft treatment or presentation treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of directorial style
rubrics_metrics.description: A treatment may include details of directorial style that an outline omits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, add notes on tone, visual style, pacing, or directorial approach to help convey the intended cinematic execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original draft treatment — purpose and content
rubrics_metrics.description: The original draft treatment is created during the writing process and is generally long and detailed. It consists of full-scene outlines put together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the draft treatment as an intermediate, comprehensive document capturing full scene-by-scene action and beats; it serves as groundwork for the first screenplay draft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original draft treatment — length and formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually there are between 30 and 80 standard letter size or A4 pages (Courier New 12 point), with an average of about 40 pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for the cited page ranges for a draft treatment; the page/format example signals expected verbosity and presentation (example: The Terminator draft treatment is 48 pages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation treatment — purpose and content
rubrics_metrics.description: The presentation treatment is created as presentation material: scene descriptions are written on index cards (or a digital equivalent) and only have the essential and important story events that make up the scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condense the story to the essential beats and master scenes; focus on concept, theme, character and the main story progression so executives or directors can grasp the idea quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation treatment — master scenes and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The presentation treatment is the full story in its simplest form, moving from the concept, to the theme, to the character, to the detailed synopsis of about four to eight pages of master scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize the presentation treatment to show concept → theme → character arc → master-scene synopsis; use master scenes to demonstrate the story’s spine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation treatment — length guidance for submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation treatments are usually at least three, but fewer than thirty, pages in length, with most being of seven to twelve pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If submitting a treatment in response to a request, follow these typical length expectations (commonly 7–12 pages) unless the submission specifies otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene-card method for structuring
rubrics_metrics.description: Scene descriptions are written out on index cards (or a digital equivalent) and are arranged and rearranged until the optimum structure is worked out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physical or digital index cards to experiment with scene order and structure; keep each card focused on the essential event(s) of a scene to aid rearrangement and structural iteration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use in adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: A treatment may also be created in the process of adapting a novel, play, or other pre-existing work into a screenplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting, use the treatment to distill the source material into a cinematic story, identifying which elements to preserve, condense, or omit for film.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to other forms (step outline, scriptment)
rubrics_metrics.description: More elaborate forms of the draft treatment are the step outline and the scriptment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of related intermediate documents: a step outline breaks the story into numbered beats/steps; a scriptment mixes prose and script elements — choose the format that best serves development or pitching needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usage as selling/pitch document
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatments are widely used within the motion picture industry as selling documents to outline story and character aspects of a planned screenplay; screenwriters may use a treatment to initially pitch a screenplay, or to sell a concept without a completed screenplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor the treatment for its audience (executives, producers, directors, buyers); when used as a sales pitch, emphasize commercial hook, character, and concise story progression.
